title: Tenali Raman and the Theft of Wells
full_text:
During a scorching summer in the empire of Vijayanagara, the capital suffered a sudden and inexplicable water shortage. While the Tungabhadra River ran low, several communal wells in the poorer artisan quarters ran completely dry overnight, leaving potters, weavers, and common laborers in distress.

Disturbed by the crisis, King Krishnadevaraya summoned his chief municipal warden, an arrogant officer named Rudrappa.
Rudrappa bowed low and offered a bizarre explanation:
'Your Majesty, the heat of the season is so intense that several public wells have cracked and mysteriously dissolved into subterranean chasms! It will require thirty thousand gold coins from the imperial treasury to construct new wells immediately!'

The King, anxious for his subjects, was about to sign the gold disbursement when Tenali Raman stepped forward with a solemn expression:
'Maharaj, the chief warden's report is profoundly alarming. Indeed, I have noticed that not only have the wells vanished, but thieves have been active under the cover of night. Just yesterday, three full stone wells were seen being carried down the western highway on the backs of thirty pack-bullocks!'

The court erupted in murmurs. King Krishnadevaraya frowned:
'Tenali, art thou mad? How can any thief steal a stone well and carry it on a bullock?'

Tenali bowed with humble gravity:
'Your Majesty, if a stone well can dissolve into thin air as the warden claims, it surely can also be dug up, loaded onto bullocks, and sold to private agricultural estates outside the city walls!'

Tenali then led the King, the ministers, and the royal guards on an unannounced inspection of the private sugarcane plantations belonging to none other than Warden Rudrappa.
There, in the lush, green fields, waterwheels were turning vigorously, pumping thousands of gallons of cool, fresh water from newly dug underground conduits that secretly diverted water from the public city wells! Rudrappa had been selling public water to wealthy orchardists at extortionate prices!

Caught red-handed, Rudrappa fell to his knees in the mud, trembling and confessing his fraud.
King Krishnadevaraya ordered the diversion canals broken immediately, returning abundant water to the artisan quarters. Rudrappa was dismissed and fined double the cost of public repairs.

The King laughed heartily and rewarded Tenali with a gold necklace:
'Only Tenali could use a thief's own impossible tale to catch him in the act!'
moral: Corrupt officials who siphon public resources find their embezzlement exposed when forced to follow their own absurd excuses.

title: The Two Thieves and the Garden Irrigation
full_text:
In Vijayanagara lived two notorious burglars, Kalu and Malu, who boasted across the taverns that no lock in the capital could resist their iron picks. Hearing that King Krishnadevaraya had rewarded Tenali Raman with a hefty purse of gold coins for his poetic compositions, the two scoundrels targeted Tenali’s modest suburban house.

One moonlit night, while sitting in his backyard veranda, Tenali noticed the shadows of two men crouching behind the dense mango trees near his boundary wall. Recognizing them as burglars biding their time until the household fell asleep, Tenali did not panic or shout for the watchmen.

Instead, he walked into the bedroom and spoke to his wife, Sharada, in a loud, anxious voice that carried clearly across the quiet yard:
'Sharada! The city is swarming with dangerous thieves tonight! It is unsafe to keep our gold and jewels inside the wooden chest under our cot. Let us pack all our gold coins, silver platters, and ancestral ornaments into the heavy iron-bound trunk. We shall drop it into the deep stone well in our backyard; the water will hide it safely until the morning patrol arrives!'

The two thieves lurking behind the mango trees grinned with greedy delight, nudging each other:
'Listen to the fool! He is dropping his entire fortune straight into the well! We won't even need to pick a lock!'

Tenali and his wife dragged a massive, iron-reinforced wooden trunk into the yard. Tenali had secretly filled it with heavy granite paving stones from his garden path. With a loud heave and a magnificent splash, they dropped the trunk into the deep well:
*KLA-BAM!*
'There,' Tenali sighed loudly. 'Now our fortune is secure. Let us sleep in peace.'
He latched the back door and blew out the oil lamp.

As soon as the house was dark, Kalu and Malu crept out of the shadows.
The well was deep and full of water. To reach the submerged iron trunk, they had to bail out the water.
Grabbing the heavy leather buckets and ropes attached to the well's wooden pulley, the two thieves began hauling water with frantic urgency.
They poured bucket after bucket onto the garden ground.
Tenali quietly opened his back bedroom window, which overlooked the garden, and watched with immense satisfaction. Whenever the water flooded one flowerbed, Tenali disguised his voice in the dark, whispering like a gust of wind:
'A bit more to the brinjal patch on the left, brothers! The jasmine creepers on the right look thirsty as well!'

All through the cool night, the two thieves hauled and poured, sweating, gasping, their muscles aching, until they had bailed out hundreds of buckets of water, thoroughly irrigating every single vegetable bed, mango sapling, and flowerbed in Tenali’s extensive garden!

Just as the first pink rays of dawn broke over the horizon, the water level dropped enough to reveal the trunk.
Exhausted and covered in mud, Kalu and Malu dragged the heavy iron box out of the sludge and pried open the lid with their crowbars.
Inside, beneath the wet straw, lay nothing but jagged granite stones!

At that moment, Tenali stepped out onto the veranda with a silver tray bearing two cups of steaming hot ginger tea.
He smiled warmly:
'Good morning, friends! My garden has never been so thoroughly irrigated! You have saved me three weeks of hard labor. Drink this warm tea before the royal guards arrive to escort you to the palace!'

The two exhausted burglars collapsed onto the wet grass in utter defeat, realizing they had spent the entire night doing honest gardening labor for the wittiest man in Vijayanagara.
moral: A clever mind turns an attempted burglary into free labor, proving that wit effortlessly outsmarts greed.

title: Tenali Raman and the Riddle of the Three Dolls
full_text:
An envoy from a distant northern kingdom arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, carrying an ornate rosewood box lined with crimson silk. Before King Krishnadevaraya and the assembled ministers, the envoy opened the box and placed three small, handcrafted wooden dolls upon the marble table.

The three dolls were identical in every outward respect: each was carved from the same sandalwood, dressed in identical silk robes, possessed the same height, weight, painted smile, and posture.

The foreign envoy challenged the court:
'O Emperor of the South! My sovereign sends these three figures as an intellectual tribute. Though they appear identical to the eye and the scale, one doll is worthless, one doll is of middling value, and one doll is beyond price. If your famed scholars cannot distinguish their true worth before sunset, your court must acknowledge the superiority of our academies!'

The King called upon his senior scholars, chief astrologers, and ministers.
One scholar sniffed the dolls, another weighed them with goldsmith balances, and a third examined their woodgrain with a magnifying glass. None could find the slightest difference.

Seeing the King grow uneasy, Tenali Raman stepped forward with a smile:
'Maharaj, grant me a thin, flexible piece of silver wire, and I shall reveal the true nature of each doll.'

The King commanded the wire brought.
Tenali approached the first doll. He found a tiny, almost invisible hole pierced in its ear. He inserted the silver wire into the doll's right ear.
As he gently pushed the wire forward, the tip of the wire slipped out through the doll's mouth!

Tenali explained:
'Your Majesty, this first doll represents the gossip and the slanderer. Whatever word enters his ear immediately spills out through his mouth to cause mischief and discord. He cannot keep a secret, nor can he be trusted with confidential state affairs. This doll is worthless and dangerous!'

Tenali moved to the second doll and inserted the wire into its ear.
The wire passed through the head and emerged out of the opposite ear!

Tenali declared:
'This second doll represents the shallow, inattentive listener. Whatever wise instruction enters one ear flies straight out through the other. He neither retains knowledge nor harms anyone intentionally, but he forgets all guidance. This doll is of middling value, like an indifferent acquaintance.'

Finally, Tenali inserted the wire into the ear of the third doll.
The wire went in, curled downwards into the figure's carved chest, and remained completely inside, without emerging from mouth or ear!

Tenali smiled with deep reverence:
'This third doll, Maharaj, represents the true friend, the trustworthy confidant, and the loyal minister. Whatever secret or sorrow is confided into his ear is locked forever within the quiet sanctuary of his heart. He listens with empathy, guards confidences with his life, and acts with steadfast integrity. This doll is priceless!'

The foreign envoy was stunned by Tenali’s profound philosophical insight and bowed low:
'Truly, Emperor Krishnadevaraya, the fame of Tenali Raman’s wisdom has not been exaggerated by half!'
The King rewarded Tenali with a chest of pearls, celebrating the truth that character is measured by what one guards within.
moral: True value lies not in outward appearance, but in how one handles the speech and confidences of others.

title: Tenali and the Persian Horse Trader
full_text:
A cunning horse trader from the north arrived at the gates of Vijayanagara with a sleek, glossy black mare. He brought the steed before King Krishnadevaraya, who had an immense passion for fine warhorses.

'Jahanpanah!' praised the trader with extravagant flourishes. 'This is no ordinary mare. She was bred in the windswept plains of Bactria, sired by the desert storm! She is so swift that she does not touch the grass when galloping, and she runs faster than the autumn wind itself! I offer her to your royal cavalry for the modest price of five thousand gold dinars.'

The King was dazzled by the mare's gleaming coat and spirited posture. He was on the verge of ordering the treasurer to pay the five thousand gold coins when Tenali Raman stepped forward.

'Maharaj,' said Tenali, 'if this magnificent beast is truly swifter than the autumn wind, we must witness her celestial speed before the entire city! Let the trader mount her and demonstrate her wind-like flight around the royal polo grounds.'

The trader, whose horse had merely been fed sweet molasses and polished with oil to look energetic, began to sweat:
'Noble courtier, such a divine mare does not run on common dirt tracks for entertainment; she runs only when her spirit is moved by destiny!'

Tenali smiled innocently:
'Ah, then we shall assist destiny! Let me prepare the testing track!'
Tenali ran into the palace kitchens and returned carrying a small clay pot filled with freshly ground, pungent red chili powder and dried ginger.
He walked behind the mare, stroked her flank gently, and whispered:
'Let us see if she can outrun her own shadow!'

Tenali suddenly blew a small pinch of chili powder into the air near the horse's nostrils, while waving a burning bundle of aromatic lemongrass.
The mare sneezed violently, bucked with fright, and bolted forward!
The trader, trying desperately to mount her to save his reputation, grabbed the reins. The terrified horse leaped, dragging the trader through a muddy ditch, through a patch of prickly cactus, and finally dumping him headfirst into a heap of damp cow manure!

The horse trotted quietly to the royal stables to drink from the water trough, showing no magical speed whatsoever.
The King and the entire court erupted in uncontrollable laughter as the trader crawled out of the manure heap, his fine silk coat ruined and his pride shattered.

King Krishnadevaraya realized how close he had come to throwing away five thousand gold coins on empty boasting:
'Tenali, thy ginger and chili test has saved our treasury from a grand fraud!'
The trader was escorted out of the city gates, learning that in Vijayanagara, empty words cannot outrun practical wit.
moral: Impulsive vanity makes easy prey for swindlers; practical proof quickly exposes boastful claims.

title: Tenali Raman and the Ascetic Cat
full_text:
One season, the granaries of Vijayanagara were overrun by a sudden plague of field mice, threatening the imperial wheat reserves.
King Krishnadevaraya, determined to solve the problem decisively, issued a royal decree:
'Every household in the capital shall be provided with a kitten from the royal catteries and a daily allowance of two cups of fresh, creamy milk from the palace dairy. Each family must raise a fat, vigorous cat to hunt the mice throughout the city!'

Every courtier and citizen gladly accepted the free milk. While their families drank the rich cream, the cats grew pampered, lazy, and ignored the mice completely.

Tenali Raman also received a kitten and the daily supply of milk.
On the very first morning, Tenali poured the fresh milk into a heavy iron bowl and heated it over a blazing charcoal fire until it boiled violently.
He placed the boiling, bubbling milk before the hungry kitten.
The kitten eagerly darted its pink tongue into the liquid—and received an instant, painful scald!
The kitten shrieked, leaped backward, and fled under the cot.

From that day forward, whenever Tenali set down a bowl of milk—even when cooled to ice—the kitten would sniff the bowl from five paces away, puff out its fur in terror, and bolt in the opposite direction!
Tenali fed the cat ordinary scraps of dry roti, fish heads, and water. As a result, the lean, hungry cat roamed the house and granary, catching every mouse within reach!

Months later, King Krishnadevaraya held an imperial parade of the royal cats in the palace courtyard to inspect how well his decree had been fulfilled.
All the courtiers brought forward enormous, round, slumbering cats, bloated with sweet cream.
When mice were released from wicker cages, the pampered cats merely yawned and rolled onto their backs!

Then came Tenali Raman, holding his lean, alert cat on a string.
The King frowned: 'Tenali, thy cat is thin and wiry! Didst thou not give it the royal milk?'
'Maharaj,' replied Tenali with a straight face, 'my cat is a strict ascetic saint. It has taken a sacred vow of total renunciation and refuses to touch even a single drop of milk!'

The King laughed in disbelief: 'A cat that refuses milk? Impossible! Cats love milk more than life itself!'
The King commanded a bowl of sweet, cooled palace milk to be placed before Tenali’s cat.
The moment the bowl touched the tiles, Tenali’s cat took one look at the white liquid, remembered the boiling scald, hissed furiously, and scrambled up the King's velvet throne canopy to get away from the bowl!

The King and the courtiers stared in utter astonishment.
Tenali smiled gently:
'Your Majesty, a creature that is given too much comfort forgets its nature and purpose. The courtiers' cats grew fat on royal charity and caught no mice, while my cat, kept alert by simple fare, cleared the granaries. When rulers shower unearned luxuries upon their servants, they create idle parasites who run from their duty.'

Krishnadevaraya grasped the profound administrative lesson beneath the comedy, rewarded Tenali with a purse of gold, and revised the city’s granary policies with practical wisdom.
moral: True governance cannot be forced by unthinking decrees; blind obedience exposes the folly of impractical mandates.

title: Tenali and the Royal Dream of Gold
full_text:
An opportunistic courtier named Subba Shastri, known for his greed, sought a clever way to enrich himself at the King's expense without doing any honest labor.

One morning, Subba Shastri arrived at the royal audience hall with an exaggerated look of pious awe. He prostrated himself before King Krishnadevaraya and exclaimed:
'Jahanpanah! Last night, a celestial vision blessed my sleep! You, our divine Emperor, appeared to me in a dream surrounded by golden angels, and with your own royal hands handed me a purse containing ten thousand gold dinars as a reward for my devotion!
Our ancient scriptures state that the dreams of righteous citizens are sacred omens. Therefore, I have come to receive the ten thousand gold coins you promised me in my dream!'

King Krishnadevaraya was taken aback. While he knew the courtier was scheming, he hesitated to dismiss the religious appeal openly, fearing he might appear irreverent before the traditionalists.

Seeing the King cornered, Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, Subba Shastri’s dream is indeed an extraordinary spiritual event. In fact, on that very same night, I had an identical dream!'

Subba Shastri grinned, assuming Tenali was supporting his claim: 'Thou seest, O King? Tenali confirms the dream!'

Tenali continued calmly:
'Indeed! In my dream, Maharaj, after giving Subba Shastri the ten thousand gold dinars, you fell into a deep financial crisis. Seeing your distress, Subba Shastri generously took out his own private family savings—twenty thousand gold dinars—and handed them back to you as an emergency loan to protect the empire!
He promised to deliver the gold to the royal treasury the very next morning!'

Subba Shastri’s smile froze. His jaw dropped in horror:
'What? I... I never dreamed such a thing!'

Tenali replied with razor-sharp logic:
'Why, friend Shastri! If the King’s promise of ten thousand coins in your dream is real enough to demand real gold from the treasury, then your promise of twenty thousand coins in my dream is twice as binding!
Pay the King the remaining ten thousand dinars right now, or confess that dreams are made of smoke and have no value in an honest court!'

Subba Shastri turned white as chalk, fell to the floor, and begged for the King's forgiveness, admitting that his dream was a greedy invention.
King Krishnadevaraya roared with laughter, dismissed the greedy courtier, and praised Tenali’s unmatched presence of mind, demonstrating that fictitious claims are best paid with imaginary debts.
moral: You cannot claim real wealth from an illusion; those who demand payment for dreams must be paid with phantom coins.

title: Tenali Raman and the Royal Brinjal Curry
full_text:
In the private gardens of the palace of Vijayanagara, the royal horticulturists had cultivated a rare, experimental variety of purple brinjal (eggplant). The fruit was sweet, succulent, and had a delicate aroma found nowhere else in the kingdom.
King Krishnadevaraya was so fond of this vegetable that he declared it exclusive to the royal table, decreeing that anyone who stole or cultivated it without permission would face severe punishment.

One evening, after dining with the King, Tenali was given a small portion of the royal brinjal curry to take home.
His wife, Sharada, tasted the curry and found it sublime. She begged Tenali:
'Raman, our young son has never tasted such a delicacy! You are a favorite of the King; surely you can bring a single brinjal from the garden for our child?'

Tenali was reluctant, but moved by fatherly affection, he slipped into the garden at twilight and plucked one ripe purple brinjal.
Sharada prepared a delicious curry and served it to their little son, who ate it with joyful praise.

However, Tenali realized the danger: children are innocent and often speak the truth without thinking. If the boy mentioned the royal brinjal to the neighbors or schoolmates, disaster would strike the family!

Tenali devised an ingenious psychological plan.
That night, while the child was sleeping deeply, Tenali carried him up to the terrace roof.
Tenali and his wife took buckets of cool water and poured them gently over the roof tiles, splashing the sleeping boy.
Then Tenali flashed a polished brass tray before a lamp to simulate lightning, while Sharada rolled a heavy brass pestle across the floor to mimic the rumble of thunder!
Tenali gently shook the boy awake, shouting:
'Wake up, son! A terrifying midnight thunderstorm has struck the city! Rain is pouring through the roof! Eat this piece of sweet brinjal curry for strength, and let us hurry downstairs before the lightning strikes!'
The bewildered, sleepy child ate the morsel, saw the water splashing, heard the thunder, and was tucked back into bed.

The next day, the royal gardener noticed a missing brinjal and reported the theft. Suspicion fell upon Tenali, whose love for good food was well known.
The King summoned Tenali and his young son to court.
The King asked the boy gently: 'Little one, did your father bring you a special purple brinjal from the royal garden for dinner yesterday?'

The boy replied eagerly:
'Yes, Maharaj! We ate it at midnight during the great thunderstorm, when lightning flashed through our bedroom and rain flooded our roof!'

King Krishnadevaraya and the ministers stared at the boy, then looked outside at the bright, dry sky.
The King laughed:
'Yesterday was a clear, dry summer night without a single cloud or drop of rain in all of Vijayanagara! The poor child was having a wild, imaginative nightmare!'

The King dismissed the accusation with affectionate chuckles.
Tenali bowed gratefully, having protected his family while leaving the court in good humor, proving that foresight and wit can defuse the greatest perils.
moral: Quick wit and psychological understanding can rescue a loved one from harsh royal wrath.

title: Tenali Raman and the Golden Mangoes
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya’s elderly mother was pious and charitable. One summer afternoon, she expressed a sudden craving for ripe, sweet mangoes. The King immediately ordered a basket of the finest fruit from the countryside, but before the basket could arrive, the queen mother fell suddenly ill and passed away peacefully.

The King was overcome with intense grief and filial remorse, weeping that his mother's final earthly wish for a mango had gone unfulfilled.

Hearing of the King’s emotional vulnerability, the chief palace priests saw a golden opportunity to enrich themselves. They assembled before the mourning monarch and solemnly pronounced:
'Maharaj, your mother's soul cannot attain eternal tranquility until her unfulfilled desire is expiated through sacred charity. According to our ancestral scriptures, you must craft thirty mangoes of solid gold, each weighing fifty tolas, and distribute them to thirty learned priests along with bags of silver!'

Grief-stricken, the King readily agreed and ordered the royal goldsmiths to forge the thirty solid gold mangoes.

When Tenali Raman heard of this shameless exploitation, his blood boiled at the priests' greed.
Tenali sent a private messenger to the thirty priests:
'Revered scholars, today my late mother’s memorial anniversary also falls. I desire to offer you sacred gifts to fulfill her last unfulfilled wish. Come to my courtyard immediately after the palace distribution.'

The greedy priests were overjoyed at the thought of receiving double charity in a single day.
After collecting their heavy gold mangoes from the palace, they hurried straight to Tenali’s house.

Tenali welcomed them with excessive courtesy into his enclosed courtyard, bolted the heavy wooden gates, and summoned his two burly servants, who held glowing red-hot iron branding rods pulled from a charcoal furnace!

The priests leaped back in terror: 'Tenali! What madness is this? Why hast thou brought branding irons?'

Tenali replied with tearful solemnity:
'Revered priests, in her final days, my poor mother suffered from agonizing chronic rheumatism in her legs. The royal physicians advised that the only cure was to brand her thighs with red-hot iron rods. Alas, she died before the treatment could be applied!
Her final wish remains unfulfilled! As learned scholars, you know that whatever was unfulfilled in this life must be received by the priests on her behalf! Come, roll up your dhoyas, so my servants may brand each of you with three strokes of the glowing iron to release my mother’s soul!'

The terrified priests shrieked in horror:
'Mercy, Tenali! Are you insane? Branding with red-hot irons will burn our skin to ashes!'

Tenali glared at them with righteous fury:
'Why, holy men? If the King’s mother wished for a juicy fruit and you demanded solid gold mangoes, then when my mother wished for hot iron branding, surely hot iron rods are the only appropriate gift!'

Realizing they had been caught in their own trap of religious extortion, the humiliated priests dropped their thirty solid gold mangoes onto the courtyard stones and fled out the back gate!

Tenali gathered the thirty gold mangoes, carried them back to the King, and revealed the priests' deceit.
King Krishnadevaraya hugged Tenali with tears of relief, realizing that true filial piety is honored by honest deeds, not by feeding the boundless greed of impostors.
moral: Greedy opportunists who exploit religious rites for personal gain deserve a taste of their own medicine.

title: Tenali Raman and the Great Pundit of Kashi
full_text:
A renowned and arrogant scholar from Kashi named Vidyaranya Pandit arrived at the imperial court of Vijayanagara. He carried banners listing dozens of scholastic titles, escorted by disciples beating drums and announcing:
'Bow down before the invincible master of logic, grammar, and metaphysics! None in Bharatavarsha can stand before his philosophical debate!'

Vidyaranya challenged the court scholars of Vijayanagara to an open disputation on classical philosophy, demanding that if none dared face him, Emperor Krishnadevaraya must sign a proclamation acknowledging Kashi's intellectual supremacy and pay a tribute of ten thousand gold dinars.

The royal scholars of Vijayanagara, intimidated by the visitor's fierce reputation, lowered their heads and made excuses.
The King was mortified, fearing that the prestige of his illustrious empire would be permanently disgraced.

At the eleventh hour, Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, grant me permission to debate this scholar tomorrow morning. I shall defend the honor of Vijayanagara!'

The next morning, the grand audience hall was packed with courtiers, scholars, and foreign ambassadors.
Vidyaranya Pandit sat upon a raised silk dais, surrounded by stacks of ancient palm-leaf manuscripts.
Tenali Raman entered the hall with immense dignity, draped in the robes of a venerable grand master. In his hands, he carried a heavy bundle wrapped securely in fine crimson Benares silk and tied with a thick, coarse hemp rope.
He placed the bundle upon his desk with theatrical reverence.

Vidyaranya eyed the mysterious, imposing package with growing anxiety.
'Learned brother,' asked Vidyaranya cautiously, 'what sacred treatise is contained within that glorious silk wrapper? Upon which philosophical school shall we base our debate?'

Tenali stroked his chin and announced in a booming voice:
'This, revered Pandit, is the greatest philosophical masterpiece of our southern scholars: the immortal treatise entitled *Tilakashta Mahisha Bandhana*! We shall debate its third chapter on cosmic causality!'

Vidyaranya’s mind raced in frantic panic. *Tilakashta Mahisha Bandhana?*
He searched through forty years of memories of libraries in Kashi, Nalanda, and Mithila, but had never heard of such a text! He feared that if he confessed ignorance, his reputation as an all-knowing master would be shattered instantly.
Trembling, Vidyaranya requested a recess until the following morning to prepare his arguments.

That night, unable to find any reference to the mysterious treatise, Vidyaranya grew terrified of public humiliation. Under the cover of darkness, he packed his baggage and fled the city of Vijayanagara on his mule, leaving behind his banners and disciples!

At dawn, when the King found the challenger had fled, he turned to Tenali in amazed delight:
'Tenali, what divine, ancient book was inside that crimson silk bundle that terrified the great pundit into flight?'

Tenali laughed, unknotted the silk wrapper, and dumped its contents onto the King's table:
Inside was a small bundle of dry sesame stalks (*Tila-kashta*), tied to a rough hemp rope normally used to tether water buffaloes (*Mahisha-bandhana*)!

'Maharaj,' chuckled Tenali, 'it was merely firewood from sesame plants tied with a buffalo tether! The pretentious scholar was so blinded by his own complicated jargon that he fled from a handful of dry twigs and a rope!'

King Krishnadevaraya and the court roared with laughter, celebrating Tenali’s brilliant victory over pompous arrogance.
moral: Pretentious pedantry and inflated jargon collapse when challenged by quick wit and simple courage.

title: Tenali Raman and the Well of Truth
full_text:
A wealthy merchant of Vijayanagara named Govinda Chetty was burgled of a brass pot containing five hundred gold mohurs. The theft had occurred without any broken locks, indicating that someone familiar with the household was responsible.
Govinda approached Tenali Raman, weeping and pleading for assistance.

Tenali investigated the merchant’s mansion quietly. He noticed that the household had an ancient, disused stone well in the rear courtyard, covered with heavy timber planks. Tenali observed that the moss around the well rim was freshly scratched and disturbed.
Suspecting that the thief had hidden the heavy pot inside the well rather than risking carrying it through the city gates, Tenali devised a psychological trap.

In the presence of all five servants and relatives, Tenali solemnly announced:
'Govinda Chetty, the theft of thy gold is an omen. This evening at twilight, the Chief Astrologer and I shall perform the ancient Rite of the Sacred Well. We shall light seventy-seven oil lamps around the rim, invoke the spirits of truth, and lower a consecrated brass hook into the water. If the stolen gold is inside, the spirits will bring it to the surface before the entire neighborhood!'

The suspects listened with wide eyes.
Tenali and Govinda then left the courtyard, pretending to go to the bazaar to purchase ceremonial incense and camphor.
Instead, Tenali and four armed guards hid behind the high brick wall of the adjoining stable.

Within two hours, just as dusk fell, one of the merchant’s trusted grooms, a youth named Somu, crept into the courtyard looking around nervously.
Believing that the 'spirits of truth' would expose him during the announced ritual, Somu hurriedly pulled away the timber planks, tied a rope around his waist, lowered himself into the well, and retrieved the heavy brass pot of gold from an underwater stone niche!

As soon as Somu climbed out onto the courtyard paving stones with the dripping pot of gold in his hands, Tenali and the guards stepped out of the shadows with lanterns!

Somu dropped the pot, the gold coins clattered across the stone floor, and he fell prostrate in terror.
'Forgive me, master!' he sobbed. 'I thought the spirits would strike me dead during the ritual!'

Tenali smiled:

title: Tenali and the Weight of Cotton
full_text:
In the bustling market of Vijayanagara operated a sly wholesale trader named Manikchand, who sold raw cotton and iron tools. He devised a deceptive argument to overcharge poor weavers:
'Look at this enormous sack of soft cotton!' he would argue. 'It occupies ten times the volume of this tiny lump of iron! Therefore, maintaining and storing cotton requires ten times the effort, and a pound of cotton is worth far more than a pound of iron!'
Through this convoluted rhetoric, he cheated poor spinning women and weavers who bought raw cotton.

A delegation of distressed weavers approached Tenali Raman for help.
Tenali promised to teach the dishonest trader an unforgettable lesson.

The next morning, Tenali visited Manikchand's shop accompanied by two porters carrying a large, heavy crate.
'Master Manikchand,' said Tenali with a polite bow, 'I have heard of your deep philosophical understanding of weight and volume. I have brought a business proposition.'

Manikchand rubbed his palms greedily: 'Speak, noble courtier!'
Tenali said:
'I wish to purchase one hundred pounds of raw cotton, and in exchange, I offer you one hundred pounds of prime black iron from the royal foundry. Since both weigh exactly one hundred pounds, will you make the trade?'

Manikchand agreed, thinking he could resell the fine foundry iron to blacksmiths for high profit.
He weighed out one hundred pounds of cotton in three large jute bags, while Tenali placed the crate of one hundred pounds of iron on the floor.

As Tenali's porters loaded the cotton bags, Manikchand looked at the heavy iron crate and said:
'Now, Raman, help my servants carry this crate into my storage cellar.'

Tenali looked astonished:
'Carry it? Why, Master Manikchand! Have you forgotten your own doctrine? According to your philosophy, iron occupies very little space and is therefore trivial to store! Since you claim cotton requires ten times the handling effort, it is only fair that you carry these three enormous cotton sacks to my house yourself, while I leave this tiny iron box right here!'

Manikchand stammered: 'Wait! One hundred pounds of iron is brutally heavy!'
Tenali replied with ringing authority:
'A pound is a pound, whether of feathers or of lead, of cotton or of iron! You used the volume of cotton to justify cheating poor weavers, yet when forced to bear the reality of weight, you cry for help!
Stop manipulating honest measures, or I will have the Market Overseer smash your scales!'

The surrounding crowd of weavers cheered.
Manikchand hung his head in shame, returned the excess money to the weavers, and swore to trade with fair weights, proving that false logic dissolves before common sense.
moral: A dishonest merchant who manipulates perceptions to cheat the poor finds his own sophistry overturned by sound reason.

title: Tenali and the Horse of Two Colors
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya purchased an extraordinary Arabian steed whose coat was unique: the left side of its body was pure, snowy white, while the right side was jet black, split down the middle with geometric perfection.
The King was intensely proud of this marvel and summoned the finest court painter, Master Raghunath:
'Paint me a life-size canvas of my marvelous horse, capturing both the pure white side and the jet black side together in a single profile portrait, without showing two horses! If you succeed, you shall receive five hundred gold coins; if you fail, you shall be banished from the court!'

Poor Raghunath spent three weeks in tears. In profile, a horse can only show one flank at a time! To show both sides simultaneously in a realistic painting without distorting the animal into an ugly monster was physically impossible.

Desperate, Raghunath sought Tenali Raman’s counsel.
Tenali smiled: 'Fear not, brother artist. Lend me the King's two-colored horse for one afternoon, and prepare your finest white canvas.'

On the day of the royal audience, the King sat upon his throne expecting the finished masterpiece.
Tenali Raman entered the hall leading the horse by its reins.
To the King’s shock, the horse was completely, uniformly dark reddish-brown from ears to hooves!

The King sprang to his feet in anger:
'Tenali! What have you done to my magnificent two-colored steed? Where is the white side? Where is the black side?'

Tenali replied with serene composure:
'Maharaj, be not angry! I have merely prepared the canvas of reality!
I had the horse roll thoroughly in the red clay mud of the Tungabhadra riverbed. Now the horse is of one single, harmonious color, and Master Raghunath has painted it with absolute perfection!'

Raghunath stepped forward and unveiled a magnificent canvas depicting a glorious, uniform reddish-brown steed grazing by the river.

The King stared, bewildered:
'Tenali, you painted the mud, not my horse’s true colors!'

Tenali laughed with gentle respect:
'Precisely, Your Majesty! Just as mud can hide two distinct colors beneath one surface, so too your royal demand asked an artist to perform an unnatural impossibility! Nature created the horse with two sides that can only be seen by walking around it. When a ruler demands that art violate the laws of nature to flatter his vanity, he receives only the color of mud!'

King Krishnadevaraya realized the biting humor of his own unreasonable command. He burst into hearty laughter, rewarded both Tenali and the painter with gold coins, and washed the mud from his beloved horse, learning to appreciate nature as it was created.

title: Tenali Raman and the List of Fools
full_text:
A charming foreign merchant arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, claiming he was a certified purveyor of legendary pure-blooded horses from the steppes of Central Asia. He spoke with flowery eloquence, bowed with supreme grace, and showed the King forged certificates stamped with royal seals.

King Krishnadevaraya was so impressed by the stranger’s promises that he handed him five thousand gold dinars as an advance payment to purchase twenty prized mares, without asking for guarantors, collateral, or even his home address in Persia!
The merchant promised to return with the herd within thirty days, and rode away into the sunset.

Two weeks later, the King, in a playful mood, turned to Tenali Raman and said:
'Tenali, thou hast a keen eye for human nature. Draw up for me a parchment containing the names of the five greatest fools in the empire of Vijayanagara!'

Tenali bowed, sat at the scribe's desk, and wrote upon a fresh scroll of palm leaf.
Within an hour, he presented the scroll to the King.

King Krishnadevaraya opened the parchment, and his eyes widened in furious shock:
At the very top of the list, written in bold golden ink, was the name:
**1. Emperor Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara.**

The King slammed the scroll onto his diwan, his face reddening with anger:
'Tenali! How darest thou write my royal name as the greatest fool in the kingdom? Explain thyself before I order the guards to seize thee!'

Tenali folded his hands with unshakeable calm:
'Maharaj, with all humble reverence: who else but the greatest fool would hand five thousand gold dinars from the imperial treasury to a smooth-talking stranger whose name, family, and homeland are completely unknown, with zero collateral, expecting him to bring horses from across the ocean?'

The King frowned:
'What if the merchant returns with the twenty horses as promised? What will become of my name on your list then?'

Tenali smiled with dazzling wit:
'If that merchant returns with the twenty horses, Maharaj, I will take an eraser, remove Your Majesty’s name from the top of the list, and write the merchant’s name in its place!'

The King sat back, struck by the undeniable truth of Tenali’s logic.
Weeks turned into months, and as Tenali had predicted, the fraudulent merchant never returned with the horses.
King Krishnadevaraya embraced Tenali, acknowledging that a wise jester who tells uncomfortable truths is more valuable to an empire than a thousand flattering courtiers.

title: The Justice of the Green Parrot
full_text:
In the marketplace of Vijayanagara, two merchants—an honest grain dealer named Madhava and a scheming textile trader named Bhima—appeared before the royal magistrate claiming ownership of an extraordinarily intelligent green parrot.
The bird was capable of reciting verses, greeting customers, and calculating numbers.

Madhava wept: 'Your Honor, I raised this parrot from a fledgling; yesterday it flew out of its cage, and Bhima captured it and refuses to return it!'
Bhima shouted: 'A lie! This bird was hatched in my grandmother's garden, and has lived in my shop for five years!'

Because both men produced witnesses who swore contradictory oaths, the magistrate was baffled and referred the dispute to Tenali Raman.

Tenali had the parrot brought into the courtroom in its gilded cage.
He asked Bhima: 'What does thy parrot eat every morning?'
Bhima answered readily: 'It feeds on roasted pistachios and sweet cream, as befits a wealthy merchant's bird!'
Tenali asked Madhava: 'What does thy parrot eat?'
Madhava replied: 'Simple dry millet, green chilies, and slices of wild guava.'

Tenali then covered the cage with a dark cloth and carried it to his private garden.
He placed two wooden bowls side by side inside the cage: one containing sweet cream and pistachios, the other containing wild guava seeds and fresh green chilies.
The moment the cloth was removed, the parrot turned immediately to the green chili and guava, devouring them with eager chirps while completely ignoring the pistachios!

Next, Tenali instructed the court clerk to stand outside the closed room and drop a metal tray with a loud crash.
When the tray clattered, the parrot squawked in alarm:
*‘Madhava! Madhava! Guard the grain bins! The wind has blown the latch!’*

Tenali smiled and brought the cage back before the assembly.
'The evidence is complete,' declared Tenali. 'A bird raised on pistachios does not prefer guava seeds, and in moments of fright, it calls out the name of the master who fed it for years!'

Confronted with the parrot's own testimony, Bhima confessed his theft.
The bird was restored to Madhava, Bhima was fined thirty silver coins, and the court praised Tenali’s keen understanding that the innocent habits of living creatures cannot be bribed or perjured.

title: Tenali and the Tested Arabian Steed
full_text:
An Arabian sea-captain docked at the port of Bhatkal and brought to Vijayanagara an exquisite, pure-bred Arabian stallion named Buraq. The horse was graceful, with high-arched neck, slender limbs, and eyes like liquid fire. The captain asked four thousand gold dinars for the stallion.

Envious courtiers who had not received bribes from the sea-captain whispered poison into King Krishnadevaraya's ear:
'Maharaj, be not deceived! This horse has a secret defect: its left hind leg is weak, and it is blind in night travel. It is unfit for imperial cavalry.'

The King, hesitant to spend royal funds on a flawed beast, was about to reject the captain when Tenali Raman spoke:
'Maharaj, words of praise and words of slander are equally cheap. A warhorse is not tested by the whispers of courtiers standing safely on velvet carpets, but by the road itself. Let me test this stallion tonight on the Obstacle Course of the Seven Terraces!'

The courtiers smirked, expecting Tenali to fall and break his bones.
At midnight, under a moonless, overcast sky, Tenali arrived at the testing grounds.
He did not use a whip or spurs. He blindfolded his own eyes with a black silk scarf, mounted the Arabian stallion, and loosened the reins completely!

'Ride, Buraq!' cried Tenali.
The stallion surged forward into the pitch-black course!
Navigating winding ditches, wooden hurdles, sharp turns, and narrow stone bridges, the noble horse leaped over obstacles with breathtaking instinct, guided purely by its own extraordinary night vision and equine intelligence!
It completed the entire treacherous circuit without tripping a single peg or stumbling once, returning to the royal pavilion in flawless stride!

Tenali removed his blindfold and dismounted gracefully:
'Behold, Your Majesty! A horse that can carry a blindfolded rider through a labyrinth in the dark without a scratch has neither weak limbs nor defective sight! The only blindness present was in the envious eyes of those who sought to disparage true excellence!'

King Krishnadevaraya was overjoyed. He purchased the stallion immediately, rewarded the honest Arab captain, and punished the slanderers, while Tenali showed that genuine virtue shines brightest when put to the test.

title: Tenali Raman and the Royal Scarecrow
full_text:
A poor farmer named Venkat, whose modest sorghum fields bordered the royal hunting reserve, came to Tenali Raman in deep despair:
'Master Tenali, swarms of aggressive black crows from the royal reserve descend upon my crops every dawn. I built scarecrows of straw with clay pots for heads, but the crows sit upon their shoulders and mock me! My family will starve if the grain is eaten!'

Tenali smiled: 'Fear not, Venkat. Tomorrow morning, thy field shall have the most formidable scarecrow in all of South India!'

Tenali went to the palace wardrobe and borrowed an old ceremonial royal mantle of embroidered crimson silk, a turban adorned with imitation peacock feathers, and an old painted wooden effigy used for military drill.
Tenali dressed the wooden figure in the King's royal robes and set it up in the center of Venkat’s sorghum field.

The next morning, King Krishnadevaraya rode past the fields on his morning hunt with his royal retinue.
The King stopped his horse in shock:
There, standing knee-deep in muddy sorghum, was an effigy dressed in his exact imperial robes, waving its sleeves in the wind, with two crows perched comfortably upon its royal turban, pecking at grains!

The King was furious:
'Who has committed this treasonous insult? Dressing a dirty scarecrow in the Emperor's royal robes?'

Tenali Raman stepped out from behind a hedge, bowing with exaggerated deference:
'Maharaj, pardon this humble farmer! He sought only the greatest power in the world to protect his crops!
He reasoned: "The entire empire of Vijayanagara trembles before the Emperor’s commands. Surely, if I dress my scarecrow as the King, the crows will flee in terror!"'

The King looked from Tenali’s innocent face to the crows happily pecking seeds atop the royal turban.
Tenali added gently:
'Alas, Your Majesty! The birds have taught us a profound political truth: royal robes and golden turbans mean nothing without the living mind of justice behind them. Even crows know the difference between an empty costume of power and true majesty!'

King Krishnadevaraya’s anger melted into appreciative laughter.
He ordered the royal granaries to compensate the farmer for all lost crops, and decreed that local farmers be provided with proper protective nets.
The King hugged Tenali, learning that true authority resides in wisdom, not in embroidered silk.

title: Tenali Raman and the Divine Boon of Laughter
full_text:
In his youth, before he entered the court of Vijayanagara, Tenali was known simply as Ramakrishna, a brilliant but penniless young scholar living in the village of Tenali. Seeking purpose and livelihood, an elderly wandering sage taught him a sacred mantra of the Divine Mother, the fierce celestial guardian, and said:
'Go to the ancient hilltop shrine at midnight. Recite this mantra three million times, and the Divine Mother will appear to grant thee thy destiny.'

Ramakrishna went to the lonely stone shrine. He sat in meditation and chanted with pure devotion through stormy nights and howling winds until his mantra was complete.

Suddenly, a blinding flash of celestial lightning illuminated the sanctum.
The Fierce Guardian Mother manifested before him, majestic and terrifying, possessing a thousand radiant faces and two thousand arms bearing sacred emblems of power!

Any ordinary mortal would have fainted in superstitious dread.
Young Ramakrishna looked up at the thousand faces, then looked down at his own small hands, and suddenly burst into uncontrollable, joyous laughter:
'Ha-ha-ha! Ho-ho-ho!'

The Divine Mother frowned with thunderous astonishment:
'Insolent youth! Mortals tremble in terror before my presence, yet thou dost laugh in my face! What causes thy reckless mirth?'

Ramakrishna bowed low, still chuckling with innocent delight:
'O Blessed Mother of the Universe! Forgive me! I looked at you and was struck by a practical thought:
We poor humans have only one nose, and when we catch a common cold, we struggle with two hands to wipe it with a handkerchief.
I looked at your thousand magnificent faces and two thousand arms, and I thought: "Heavens! If the Mother of the Universe ever catches a cold, how does she manage to wipe a thousand running noses with only two thousand hands?" The picture was so delightfully humorous that I could not hold back my laughter!'

The Fierce Guardian Mother stared at the youth, and her terrifying countenance softened into a radiant, celestial smile. She burst into divine laughter that echoed across the mountains:
'Ramakrishna! Thy fearlessness, thy pure innocence, and thy razor-sharp wit have conquered my heart!
Thou didst not tremble, nor didst thou ask for gold.
Henceforth, thou shalt be known as a *Vikatakavi*—the Supreme Jester-Poet! Thy wit shall outshine the greatest scholars, thy laughter shall humble mighty kings, and thy fame shall endure as long as the stars shine in the heavens!'

Blessed with this divine gift of wit, Tenali Raman journeyed to the imperial court of Vijayanagara, where his humor and wisdom transformed an empire.
moral: Humor, presence of mind, and the courage to find joy even before awe win the favor of destiny.

title: Tenali and the Royal Portrait

title: The Challenge of the Speaking Clay Pot
full_text:
A wandering charlatan named Devasharma set up a booth outside the main temple of Vijayanagara, displaying a large, unadorned terracotta water pot. He proclaimed to the gathering crowds:
'Behold the Miraculous Speaking Pot of the Himalayas! This sacred clay vessel contains an ancient subterranean spirit who answers all questions regarding the future, speaking with a mysterious, hollow voice from within the pot!'

Citizens paid silver coins to ask questions, and indeed, a muffled, deep voice echoed from the mouth of the pot, delivering cryptic prophecies.
Even several ministers were taken in by the marvel, urging the King to consult the 'oracle'.

Tenali Raman suspected fraud. He visited the booth, stood before the crowd, and said:
'Revered Devasharma, let me ask the sacred pot three questions to verify its celestial origin.'

Devasharma agreed, confident in his deception.
Tenali approached the pot, held his ear close, and asked:
'O Spirit of the Pot! What did I eat for breakfast this morning?'
A muffled voice from the pot replied: 'Pounded rice and curd!'
Tenali asked: 'What is hidden in my left sleeve?'
The voice replied: 'A silver coin!'

Tenali nodded with a smile. He stepped back, reached into his pouch, and pulled out a small bundle of dry, pungent chili peppers and a smoldering piece of charcoal!
Before Devasharma could react, Tenali tossed the smoking chilies straight into the mouth of the clay pot!

Within three seconds, a violent fit of coughing and sneezing exploded not from the pot, but from beneath the wooden table covered by a long velvet cloth!
*‘Achoo! Achoo! Cough! Mercy! I am suffocating!’*

Tenali whipped away the velvet table cloth:
Huddled in a shallow dugout pit beneath the table was a scrawny young boy, breathing through a hollow bamboo reed that connected secretly to the bottom of the terracotta pot!

The crowd gasped in outrage at the exposed fraud.
Devasharma fell to his knees, begging for mercy, confessing that he used the ventriloquist boy to fleece gullible pilgrims.
Tenali turned to the assembly:
'Never surrender your reason to talking pots, flying carpets, or hollow voices. Heaven gave us eyes to observe and minds to discern.'

The charlatan was handed over to the municipal guards, the boy was sent to an honest trade school, and Tenali was hailed as the defender of public reason.

title: Tenali and the Leaking Temple Idol

At a prominent temple near the palace, a haughty and avaricious chief priest named Somayaji hoarded all the food offerings brought by devotees. While poor beggars starved outside the temple gates, Somayaji and his relatives feasted on mounds of ghee rice, sweet laddus, and milk puddings, throwing the surplus to stray dogs rather than sharing a single grain with the needy.

He claimed: 'The deity consumes the spiritual essence, and the sacred leftovers belong exclusively to my family by divine right!'

Tenali Raman resolved to correct this injustice.
He hired a master sculptor to craft an exact replica of the temple's stone pedestal. Inside the stone base, the sculptor carved a hidden channel leading through a small copper pipe straight out the temple foundation into an open stone trough outside the courtyard wall, where the poor sat.

Tenali then donated a magnificent, large bronze vessel to the temple, placing it before the altar directly over the concealed drain.

The next morning, when devotees poured hundreds of pots of sweet milk, honey, and clarified butter over the altar, the liquids flowed into the bronze vessel and immediately drained through the concealed channel straight into the stone trough outside!
The hungry beggars and orphans outside the wall joyfully filled their clay cups with fresh milk and honey, drinking to their hearts' content!

Inside, Somayaji stood with his empty copper pots, staring in utter bewilderment:
'Heavens! Where has all the milk gone? The altar is completely dry!'

Tenali, who was standing among the worshippers, proclaimed loudly:
'Rejoice, citizens of Vijayanagara! For forty years, the priest claimed the deity only ate spiritual essence. But today, the deity has grown so compassionate that it has drunk all the milk physically, and miraculously poured it straight into the mouths of the hungry children outside!'

The entire crowd ran outside and saw the happy children drinking. They cheered and praised the miracle!
When Somayaji inspected the altar and discovered the hidden pipe, he angrily confronted Tenali.
Tenali looked at him with unwavering moral clarity:
'Somayaji, the true altar of the divine is the hungry stomach of an innocent child. If your prayers cannot teach you to feed the poor, a hollow stone pipe will do the work for you!'

Ashamed before the entire city and fearing the King's censure, the priest reformed his ways, instituting a daily communal kitchen for the poor that distributed temple food freely to all in need.

A wandering ascetic named Siddha Govinda arrived in Vijayanagara, boasting in the marketplace that he possessed a 'Miraculous Mango Seed' blessed by Himalayan hermits.
'Plant this seed in the ground,' he boasted, 'chant my secret mantra, and within one hour it will sprout, grow into a mature tree, blossom, and bear sweet ripe mangoes before your eyes! But beware: the tree will only grow for a man whose heart is free from every trace of foolishness!'

King Krishnadevaraya, intrigued by the claim, invited the ascetic to the palace gardens to perform the miracle before the court.

The ascetic dug a small hole in the lawn, placed a dried mango seed inside, covered it with soil, and sprinkled scented water.
He then turned to the King and said:
'Now, Maharaj, you must step forward and chant the sacred syllable. But remember: if you have ever committed a single foolish act in your life, the seed will rot and never sprout!'

The King hesitated, feeling uneasy: 'As a ruler, I have made hasty decisions in my youth. I cannot claim never to have been foolish.'
The ascetic turned to the Prime Minister, Appaji:
'Then let the Prime Minister chant!'
Appaji smiled wryly: 'Alas, I once bought a broken boat from a merchant; I, too, am not completely free of folly.'
One by one, the ministers and courtiers stepped back, confessing past mistakes.

The ascetic smirked triumphantly, preparing to collect his bag of gold for proving the court unworthy.
At that moment, Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Give me the watering cup! I shall chant the mantra, for I have never committed a single foolish act in my life!'

The courtiers gasped. Tenali poured the water, chanted loudly, and waited.
One hour passed. Two hours passed. The sun climbed high.
The ground remained completely flat and bare: not a single green shoot appeared!

The ascetic sneered: 'Aha! Tenali Raman, thou hast lied! Thou art a fool, for the seed refused to sprout!'

Tenali laughed with booming joy:
'Indeed, friend ascetic! I was foolish enough to stand in the hot sun for two hours waiting for a dry mango seed to turn into a tree in sixty minutes!
And every courtier here was foolish enough to believe that nature violates its eternal seasons for your empty chant!
Trees require fertile soil, regular watering, patient months of sunlight, and honest labor to bear fruit. Whosoever expects sweet mangoes without honest farming is the greatest fool of all!'

The King and the ministers burst into laughter at Tenali’s brilliant demonstration.
The charlatan ascetic packed his dry seeds and fled the city, while the King planted real mango saplings in the royal orchards, learning that patient nature outshines all fraudulent shortcuts.
moral: Those who boast of supernatural miracles to justify laziness are humbled when confronted with natural reality.

title: Tenali Raman and the Growing Sticks
full_text:
A wealthy diamond merchant of Vijayanagara named Keshava Murthy hosted a grand dinner for his seven trusted household clerks. That night, a velvet bag containing fifty precious uncut gems disappeared from his iron safe.
The safe had been unlocked with a duplicate key, proving that one of the seven clerks was the thief.
Distressed, the merchant sought Tenali Raman’s counsel.

Tenali gathered the seven clerks in a private hall. He looked into each man’s eyes: all protested their innocence with loud oaths.
Tenali smiled calmly:
'Brothers, since human witnesses are absent, we must rely upon the ancient Magic Bamboo of Justice.'

Tenali produced seven identical polished bamboo sticks, each precisely twelve inches long.
He handed one stick to each clerk:
'These sticks have been blessed with ancient forensic mantras. Take your stick home tonight and place it beneath your sleeping mat.
Tomorrow morning at sunrise, return here with your stick.
Whosoever is innocent will find his stick unchanged. But whosoever stole the gems will find that his stick has miraculously grown by two inches overnight!'

The clerks took their sticks and departed.
Six of the clerks, whose consciences were completely clear, slept peacefully through the night, paying no heed to their sticks.

However, the seventh clerk, a man named Raghavan who had indeed stolen the gems, tossed and turned in terror.
He reasoned to himself:
'If my stick grows by two inches overnight, Tenali will identify me immediately! But if I take a sharp knife and cut exactly two inches off the end of my stick right now, when it grows two inches tonight, it will measure twelve inches again by morning, and no one will ever know!'

Raghavan took a kitchen knife, carefully sawed two inches off his stick, polished the cut edge with sandpaper, and went to sleep feeling extraordinarily clever.

The next morning, the seven clerks assembled before Tenali Raman and the merchant.
Tenali commanded each man to hold his stick against a certified bronze measuring ruler.
The first stick: exactly twelve inches.
The second: twelve inches.
The third, fourth, fifth, and sixth: all twelve inches.

Then Raghavan stepped forward and handed his stick to Tenali.
Tenali laid it against the ruler: it measured exactly **ten inches**!

Tenali grasped Raghavan’s wrist and announced:
'Behold the thief! The sticks had no magic to grow; the only magic was in the thief’s own guilty terror!'

Raghavan fell to the floor weeping, confessed his crime, and led the guards to his garden where the velvet bag of diamonds was buried intact.
The merchant rewarded Tenali handsomely, marveling at how psychological insight can make a criminal convict himself.
moral: Guilt creates its own paranoia; a thief's own fear of detection unmasks him without a witness.

title: Tenali Raman and the Cure for the King's Cold
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya was struck by a severe head cold and throat congestion. He lay in his royal bedchamber, wrapped in heavy woolen shawls, his nose red, his eyes watering, coughing and grumbling in foul humor.
The royal physicians prepared bitter herbal decoctions of black pepper, neem, and ginger, but the King spat them out, refusing to drink the foul-tasting draughts, shouting at his ministers and threatening to banish his doctors.

The royal household walked on tiptoe, terrified of provoking the irritable monarch.
Tenali Raman entered the bedchamber carrying no medicine bowls or herbs, but wearing an absurd, oversized turban made of a braided straw floor mat, balanced precariously with a giant yellow pumpkin tied to its peak!

The King blinked his watery eyes, glared at Tenali, and croaked:
'Tenali! What is that ridiculous monstrosity on your head? Have you come to mock your suffering Emperor?'

Tenali bowed with exaggerated solemnity, wobbling the heavy pumpkin:
'Maharaj! I have consulted the greatest veterinarian of the royal elephant stables! He assured me that your cold was caused by an excess of heavy thoughts weighing down your royal head.
To balance the cosmic humors, I have worn this pumpkin hat, and I have brought the imperial royal decree of elephant etiquette!'

Tenali pulled out an enormous palm leaf and began reading fabricated royal rules in an absurd, nasal, high-pitched voice:
'Rule Number One: Any elephant that sneezes in the presence of the King must bow thrice, wipe its trunk with a silk handkerchief measuring forty cubits, and recite a poem in praise of mangoes!
Rule Number Two: Any physician who prepares bitter neem soup must first drink three buckets of his own potion in the public square while balancing a goose on his forehead!'

The mental image of the dignified court physicians balancing geese while drinking buckets of neem soup was so overwhelmingly hilarious that King Krishnadevaraya could no longer contain himself.
A snort escaped his nose, followed by a chuckle, and then the Emperor burst into roaring, body-shaking, tearful laughter:
'Ha-ha-ha! Ho-ho-ho! Stop, Tenali, stop! My ribs are aching!'

As the King laughed uproariously, his chest opened, he sneezed three tremendous sneezes that cleared his blocked nasal passages completely, and his heavy headache vanished!
He wiped his eyes, breathed deeply without coughing, and realized with astonishment that his throat was clear and his fever was broken!

The King sat up in bed, energized and refreshed:
'Tenali, your absurd pumpkin hat and witty prescription have done what forty bowls of bitter medicine could not! Laughter is indeed the sovereign remedy of nature!'
The King rewarded Tenali with a basket of sweet apples, proving that joy and humor possess genuine healing power.
moral: Hearty laughter and joyful spirits are the most potent medicine for both bodily ailments and mental gloom.

title: Tenali Raman and the Persian Linguist
full_text:
A proud linguist and ambassador from the court of the Shah of Persia, named Mirza Baig, visited Vijayanagara. He was fluent in several Middle Eastern languages, but spoke only classical Persian at the court, refusing to speak a single word of the local Telugu or Kannada languages.
Through his interpreter, Mirza boasted:
'Your Majesty, Persian is the language of angels, kings, and refined poetry. None in your southern kingdom possesses the intellectual refinement to understand its profound cadences or converse with me!'

The court scholars were embarrassed, having studied primarily Sanskrit and regional tongues.
King Krishnadevaraya, unwilling to let his court appear uncultured, looked anxiously toward Tenali Raman.

Tenali stepped forward, smiled warmly at the Persian scholar, and bowed with grand courtly gestures.
Tenali cleared his throat and addressed Mirza Baig in a rapid, energetic stream of words that sounded remarkably like Persian:
'Khuda-ba-khud, nishast-o-barkhast, qalami-kalam, mirza-salam!
Tungabhadra-paani, mirza-hairaani!
Katori-mein-shakar, mirza-chakkar!'

Mirza Baig listened intently, his eyes widening in shock. The rhythm, the nasal cadences, and the rhyming inflections were delivered with such majestic confidence and perfect Persian inflection that Mirza assumed Tenali was reciting an obscure, highly philosophical Persian proverb on hospitality and river currents!

Mirza bowed low with deep respect:
'Masha'Allah! What profound philosophical synthesis! You have encapsulated the essence of friendship and the flow of rivers in four sublime lines!'
Mirza presented Tenali with an expensive embroidered Persian shawl and a silver pen-case, praising the scholarly depth of Vijayanagara before departing in awe.

When the Persian ambassador was safely outside the city, King Krishnadevaraya turned to Tenali in astonishment:
'Tenali! When did you learn classical Persian? What did those verses mean?'

Tenali burst into laughter, wrapping the Persian shawl around his shoulders:
'Maharaj, I know not a single word of real Persian!
I merely took five common Hindustani bazaar words—"Kalam" (pen), "Shakar" (sugar), "Paani" (water), and "Salam" (greeting)—and mixed them with our local river Tungabhadra, rhyming them with "Mirza's dizziness" (Mirza-chakkar)!
The Persian scholar was so eager to find profound poetry that his own imagination translated my nonsensical bazaar rhymes into celestial wisdom!'

The King and the courtiers roared with laughter, marveling at how Tenali’s linguistic audacity and understanding of human nature had outsmarted foreign arrogance.
moral: True mastery of language lies in mutual understanding and situational wit, not in showing off foreign vocabulary.

title: Tenali and the Washerman's Donkey
full_text:
In a neighborhood along the riverbanks of Vijayanagara lived a harsh washerman named Devappa, who owned an old, faithful grey donkey. Although the beast had carried mountainous bundles of wet clothes for fifteen years, Devappa beat it mercilessly with an iron-tipped stick and gave it only dry thistle scraps to eat.
One evening, bruised and starving, the donkey slipped its tether and wandered into the forest.

The next morning, Devappa came weeping to Tenali Raman, begging for help:
'Master Tenali, my donkey is gone! Without him, I cannot deliver laundry to the palace courtiers! Help me find him!'

Tenali, who had long observed Devappa’s cruelty to the beast, resolved to teach the washerman an unforgettable lesson.
Tenali went into the forest, found the gentle donkey grazing peacefully near a pond, and led it to an empty stable behind his house.
Using non-toxic yellow turmeric paste and black charcoal soot, Tenali painted bold, ferocious tiger stripes across the donkey’s grey coat!
He then tied a large brass cowbell inside a burlap bag around its neck.

That evening, Tenali told Devappa:
'Devappa, a ferocious striped mountain beast with a booming bell has taken shelter in the rocky ravine near thy house. Go and capture it!'

Devappa approached the ravine with a wooden cudgel.
Suddenly, out trotted the striped donkey, shaking its brass bell.
In the moonlight, the beast appeared like a monstrous, demon-striped tiger!
Devappa threw down his cudgel, screaming in terror:
'Help! A man-eating tiger has come to devour me!'
He fell onto his knees, trembling, weeping, and begging the heavens for mercy:
'I have been a cruel wretch! I beat my poor donkey! Spare my life, O tiger king!'

At that moment, the donkey looked at its trembling master, opened its mouth, and let out a familiar, resounding bray:
*‘HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW! HAW-HAW!’*

Tenali Raman stepped out from behind the trees with a lantern:
'Look closely, Devappa! Is this a man-eating tiger, or the gentle friend who carried thy laundry for fifteen years?'

Devappa wiped his eyes, recognizing his donkey beneath the yellow turmeric stripes.
He was overcome with profound shame and relief.
He embraced the donkey, fed it sweet jaggery and fresh grass, and swore never again to raise a stick against the faithful beast, having learned that those who serve us deserve compassion and respect.
moral: Cruelty and neglect toward faithful working beasts invite poetic justice that teaches gratitude.

title: Tenali Raman and the Merchant of Dreams
full_text:
A traveling trickster named Mayan arrived in the bustling market of Vijayanagara, setting up an opulent velvet tent adorned with colored glass lanterns. He proclaimed to the curious townspeople:
'I am the Master Dream Merchant! For a single gold coin, I will sell you a fragrant herbal incense that will grant you whatever dream you desire—to be an emperor, to discover mountains of emeralds, or to fly across the stars!'

Many foolish youths and gullible citizens paid gold coins, burned the incense, dreamed extravagant dreams, and woke up to find their purses empty and their daily chores neglected.

Tenali Raman decided to bring an end to this deceptive trade.
He walked into the tent, paid one gold coin, and said:
'Master Mayan, sell me a dream of becoming the sole sovereign of Vijayanagara, seated upon the Golden Throne, commanding all the treasuries and armies.'

Mayan handed Tenali a pinch of scented sandalwood powder: 'Burn this tonight, and thy dream is guaranteed!'

The next morning, Tenali arrived at the tent accompanied by four royal guards with drawn swords!
Tenali pointed at Mayan: 'Arrest this man for high treason!'

Mayan trembled in terror: 'Treason? What have I done, Master Tenali?'
Tenali declared in a booming, authoritative voice:
'Last night, I burned thy incense. In my dream, I became the absolute Emperor of Vijayanagara! As Emperor, I reviewed the royal accounts and discovered that thou hast been operating an illegal lottery within my empire without paying the imperial license fee of five thousand gold dinars!
Pay the five thousand gold dinars to the imperial guards immediately, or be marched to the citadel dungeon!'

Mayan cried out in despair:
'Master Tenali! It was only a dream! How can you arrest a real man for a decree issued in a dream?'

Tenali smiled with razor-sharp irony:
'Why, Master Merchant? If thy dreams are real enough to demand real gold coins from innocent citizens, then the imperial decrees issued inside those dreams are real enough to demand real fines!
Confess that dreams are illusions of no commercial value, return every stolen coin to the people, and leave Vijayanagara forever!'

Terrified, the Dream Merchant unlocked his iron cashbox, returned every single gold coin to the cheated townspeople, packed his tent, and fled the empire.
The citizens cheered Tenali, realizing that those who profit from illusions must be defeated with their own phantoms.
moral: Deceptive peddlers who sell imaginary illusions must be paid with mirror reflections.

title: The Price of a Cup of Buttermilk
full_text:
On a scorching summer afternoon, an elderly village woman named Gangamma walked three miles carrying a heavy earthen pot of fresh, cool buttermilk seasoned with curry leaves and ginger to the royal plaza. She sold cups of buttermilk for a single copper coin to parched porters and travelers.

An arrogant and haughty courtier named Somappa, dressed in lavish silk robes, strutted past. He demanded a large brass cup of cold buttermilk, drank it in one thirsty gulp, and tossed the cup back without paying.
When Gangamma asked for her copper coin, Somappa sneered:
'Old hag! Thou shouldst be honored that an imperial courtier drank from thy dirty earthen pot! Away from my path before I have my servants overturn thy stall!'

Gangamma began to weep. Tenali Raman, who was walking across the plaza, witnessed the injustice.
Tenali gently wiped the old woman's tears: 'Mother, sit in the shade. Somappa shall pay for thy buttermilk with interest.'

Tenali hurried to the palace and entered King Krishnadevaraya's audience hall, where Somappa was boasting of his lineage.
Tenali bowed:
'Maharaj, today I observed a miraculous demonstration of ancient culinary alchemy in the marketplace! Courtier Somappa has mastered the secret art of churning buttermilk so efficiently that a single cup can generate the strength of ten elephants!
He claims that churning butter is so effortless that he can churn an entire barrel of thick cream within two hours without breaking a sweat!'

The King, intrigued, looked at Somappa: 'Is this true, Somappa?'
Somappa, too proud to contradict Tenali in the presence of the Emperor, puffed out his chest: 'Of course, Your Majesty! For an aristocrat of my vigor, manual churning is child's play!'

Tenali smiled: 'Splendid! The palace kitchen has four barrels of thick buffalo curd waiting to be churned for tonight’s banquet. Let Somappa demonstrate his prowess before the court!'

A massive wooden churn and heavy rope were set up in the hot palace courtyard.
Somappa was forced to take off his fine silk coat and grip the rough hemp ropes.
For two grueling hours under the blazing afternoon sun, Somappa pulled and hauled, back and forth, back and forth!
His soft, unaccustomed hands blistered, his silk dhoti was splattered with sour cream, his breath came in ragged wheezes, and sweat poured like rain into his eyes!
Whenever he stopped, Tenali called out cheerfully:
'Keep pulling, noble courtier! The King is watching from the balcony!'

By the time the golden butter finally separated, Somappa collapsed onto the stone floor, completely exhausted, clutching his blistered palms.
Tenali handed him a cup of cold water and said softly:
'Now, Somappa, thou knowest what sweat, toil, and blistered hands go into making a single pot of buttermilk.
When poor old Gangamma walks three miles in the sun carrying her pot, a single copper coin is not just money; it is her very life and dignity.'

Somappa, humiliated and genuinely remorseful, reached into his purse and handed Gangamma ten gold coins for her cup of buttermilk.
The King praised Tenali’s lesson in the dignity of labor, decreeing that working artisans and vendors must be treated with unwavering courtesy throughout the empire.
moral: Arrogant nobility who despise the hard labor of working women are humbled when forced to sweat at the churn.

title: Tenali Raman, the Elephant, and the Mouse
full_text:
The Commander-in-Chief of the Vijayanagara army, General Veerabhadra, was excessively proud of the royal war elephant, Airavata. The beast was an immense tusker standing twelve feet tall, armored in steel plates, and trained to shatter fortress gates.
The General boasted:
'Airavata is invincible! Nothing on earth can make him turn back or tremble! He fears neither fire, nor arrows, nor lions!'

Tenali Raman smiled quietly from the pavilion:
'General, the universe is full of mysteries. The largest mountain can be moved by a hidden fault, and the mightiest giant often trembles before the smallest creature. I can make your invincible Airavata flee in terror using a creature no larger than a betel nut!'

The General laughed scornfully:
'Tenali, thou art a jester who talks nonsense! If thou canst make Airavata take a single step backward with a creature the size of a betel nut, I will surrender my jeweled sword to thee!'

The wager was accepted before King Krishnadevaraya.
The next morning, the immense war elephant was brought to the parade grounds, trumpeting fiercely, surrounded by armored cavalry.

Tenali Raman walked into the arena carrying a tiny, woven wicker box.
He walked directly in front of the towering tusker.
The elephant raised its trunk, preparing to crush the tiny man.
Tenali opened the wicker box and released a tiny, energetic grey field mouse onto the sand!

The little mouse, terrified by the thundering noise, scurried straight toward the elephant's massive front foot, seeking shelter near the shadow of its toenails.
The moment Airavata’s sensitive eyes saw the tiny creature darting toward its feet, the elephant’s ancient equine and pachyderm instinct took over:
Elephants possess an intense, instinctual terror that small creatures might crawl up their sensitive, nerve-packed trunks!

Airavata let out a shrill, panic-stricken squeal:
*‘TRUMP-EEEET!’*
The colossal beast scrambled backward, trampled the decorative flags, knocked over the commander's reviewing canopy, and bolted out of the arena at top speed, splashing into the river shallows to get away from the tiny mouse!

The entire audience erupted in roaring laughter.
General Veerabhadra stood frozen in utter mortification.
Tenali picked up the tiny mouse, placed it safely back into its wicker box, and bowed to the King:
'Maharaj, nature has designed the world with perfect balance. The mighty must never despise the weak, nor should size be mistaken for absolute invulnerability. A tiny thorn can bring down a champion, and a little mouse can rout an armored tusker!'

The King rewarded Tenali with a gold medal, and the General learned a lifelong lesson in humility.
moral: True strength does not lie in colossal size; even the mightiest fear the smallest unexpected danger.

title: The Two Brothers and the Laughing Field
full_text:
Two farmer brothers, Somanna and Bhimanna, came before King Krishnadevaraya’s court, arguing furiously over the inheritance of a fertile five-acre agricultural field left by their late father.
Somanna shouted: 'The eastern half has the canal water; it belongs to me by birthright!'
Bhimanna yelled: 'The western half has rich black soil; our father promised it to me on his deathbed!'

They produced contradictory witnesses, spent their savings on dishonest lawyers, and neglected the land completely, until the once-blooming field became overgrown with thorny weeds and scrub.

The King, exhausted by their endless bickering, turned to Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, settle this dispute equitably, for they have disrupted the court for three months.'

Tenali had both brothers brought before him. He asked:
'Brothers, have you asked the field itself to whom it wishes to belong?'
The brothers stared: 'Can a patch of dirt speak?'
Tenali replied solemnly:
'The Earth is a living mother; she speaks to those who listen. Let us go to the field at sunset.'

At the field, Tenali knelt upon the soil, placed his ear against the dry ground, and listened intently for ten minutes while the brothers watched in silence.

Tenali stood up, brushing dirt from his knees, with a sorrowful expression:
'Brothers, I heard the field speaking clearly.'
Somanna asked eagerly: 'What did she say? Did she award the land to me?'
Bhimanna asked: 'Did she name me her owner?'

Tenali answered:
'The field was laughing aloud with bitter mockery!
She said: "Behold these two foolish brothers! For ten generations, their ancestors claimed they owned me; each man died, turned to dust, and became part of my soil, while I remained here eternal and unchanged!
Today, these two sons fight and bleed over who owns me, yet neither of them has planted a single seed of corn or given me a drop of water for a whole year!
Tell them: I belong not to the man who waves a stamped paper of ownership, but to the hands that till my soil, plant seeds with love, and feed the hungry with honest sweat!"'

The two brothers stood in stunned silence.
Tenali’s profound words pierced through their selfish arrogance like an arrow of light.
They looked at the neglected, weed-choked field that had fed their ancestors for centuries, and tears of shame filled their eyes.

Somanna embraced Bhimanna, dropping their lawsuits on the spot.
They agreed to divide the work equally, sharing water and soil as partners. Within a season, the field was green with bumper crops of golden paddy, proving that true ownership is earned through loving care, not angry contention.
moral: Earth yields its treasure not to legal squabbles, but to honest labor that nurtures it with love.
